extracted.intended_audience: law students, agency lawyers/staff, and members of the public who participate in federal notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance summarizing federal administrative rulemaking procedures under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), including informal (notice-and-comment), formal (hearing-on-the-record), negotiated rulemaking tracks, exceptions, and judicial review. Useful for people who draft rules, prepare comments, or challenge/defend agency rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and function of rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking is the process by which administrative agencies adopt binding rules of general applicability as a means of furthering the statutory mandate of the agency; it serves a legislative function and implements prospective policies applicable to broad ranges of cases (in contrast to adjudication, which is retroactive and limited in scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why rulemaking procedures differ from adjudicatory protections (e.g., due process does not apply to rulemaking in the same way).

rubrics_metrics.name: APA procedural baseline and tracks
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA prescribes procedures agencies must adopt when they engage in rulemaking; most proposed rules follow informal rulemaking (notice and comment), but the APA also provides for formal rulemaking when a statute calls for a 'hearing on the record.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress may add procedural requirements beyond APA for specific agencies. Courts interpret 'hearing on the record' strictly; mere statutory reference to a 'hearing' does not always trigger formal rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice content and publication requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of a proposed rule must be published in the Federal Register and include details regarding the time, place and nature of the proceeding, a reference to the legal authority giving the agency authority, and a description of the substance of the proposed rule and the issues involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if all those who would be subject to the new rule are mentioned by name and are served with notice, publication in the Federal Register is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment opportunity and format
rubrics_metrics.description: During the public comment period, interested parties may submit written data, views or arguments to the agency; oral presentations are not required by the APA but agencies commonly hold open meetings and now generally accommodate electronic communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments may be posted on the agency website so parties can track arguments and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose critical findings and data
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must disclose to the public any critical findings or data relevant to the proposed rule so that those who wish to comment can do so in a meaningful and informed manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency fails to disclose critical material (or learns of new material after the comment period and does not disclose it), courts may overturn the rule for insufficiency of public opportunity to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of comment period length
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of time afforded for the comment period must be reasonable, though that determination depends on the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is 'reasonable' is context-dependent; agencies should tailor comment periods to the complexity and stakes of the rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to proposal and 'logical outgrowth' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may alter the proposed rule from its initial published form in response to public comment and are not required to re-issue notice and allow a further comment period so long as the changes are a 'logical outgrowth' of the proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring a new comment period for every modification would discourage agencies from incorporating public comment; if changes are not a logical outgrowth, courts may require additional notice/comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of basis and purpose in the final rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When adopting a final rule, the agency must include a statement of the basis and purpose of the rule as part of the final version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement must address significant and material objections raised by the public during the comment period and provide explanations of how the issues raised by the comments were considered and resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and effective date rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a rule has been adopted, it typically must be published in the Federal Register thirty days before it goes into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain rules may go into effect immediately upon publication — the page lists examples such as substantive rules which recognize an exemption to a policy, interpretive rules explaining statutory meanings, and policy rules explaining how agencies will exercise discretion. (Agencies must still follow statutory/APA timing requirements where applicable.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-adoption petitions and agency responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Following adoption, agencies must allow interested parties to petition for amendment or repeal of a rule; the APA requires only that the agency give prompt notice of any denial with a brief statement of the grounds of the denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts uphold denials as long as they have a rational basis and the agency has 'adequately explained' the facts and policies relied on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review and remedies for unlawful rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A final course of appeal against an administrative rule is to seek judicial remedy from a federal court; if the court finds the agency action substantively or procedurally invalid, it must set aside the rule as unlawful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may alternatively remand the case to the agency to reconsider legally problematic aspects, allowing the agency to remedy and re-adopt the rule using lawful means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on courts imposing additional procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: While courts may review agency decisions for compliance with APA procedures, courts may not impose additional procedural requirements on agency rulemaking procedures other than those prescribed by the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation is intended to preserve clear and predictable procedures and to avoid forcing agencies into more judicial-type hearings that would reduce efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for rules of agency organization/procedure/practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules concerning agency organization, procedure or practice need not follow the notice and comment provisions of the APA and may be adopted with notice to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if such a procedural rule or policy statement impacts a substantive legal right, the exemption does not apply and the agency must follow the rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause exception to notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA recognizes a 'good cause' exception under which an agency may enact a policy without notice and comment if it finds that such a process would be impractical, unnecessary or contrary to the public interest; the agency must include an explanation of the good cause it relied on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One common example is emergency rules regulating health or public safety conditions; courts examine the agency's justification for invoking good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory exemptions (military, foreign affairs, management, benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA sets forth exceptional cases where the government may proceed without applying the rulemaking provisions, including circumstances involving military or foreign affairs, agency management or personnel, or public loans, grants or benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: limiting total amount a hospital can charge Medicare patients was treated as a benefits-related action that did not require informal rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility and limits of ex parte contacts during rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Ex parte contact (communication between outside parties and agency officials) is not prohibited in rulemaking (unlike adjudication), so interested parties may engage agency officials outside the public record unless otherwise prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits arise when the rulemaking outcome is akin to resolving a dispute between two parties—then courts may treat it more like adjudication and ex parte contacts may jeopardize the rule. If a rule appears to be the product of private agreement with little public opportunity, it may be challengeable. Some agencies require disclosure of such contacts to mitigate unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal rulemaking (hearing-on-the-record) procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a statute stipulates that a proposed rule requires a hearing on the record, the APA provisions for formal rulemaking apply: publication in the Federal Register, judicial-type hearings before an Administrative Law Judge (or presiding official), with powers including issuing subpoenas, ruling on evidentiary matters, and requiring parties to attempt ADR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may submit oral or documentary evidence, cross-examine witnesses; all evidence becomes part of the official record which forms the basis for the decision. Ex parte contact is not permitted during formal rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiated rulemaking requirements and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Under negotiated rulemaking, an agency may invite interested parties to work with agency representatives to devise new rules (useful when there are a limited number of identifiable interests). The agency must publish notice of negotiated rulemaking in the Federal Register, including details of the proposed committee, agenda, and timetable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 30-day public comment process addresses the proposed negotiated rulemaking and committee composition; if the committee reaches agreement, the proposal is published as a proposed rule and the usual notice-and-comment process follows. The agency is not bound to adopt the committee's agreed proposal and may propose an alternative after negotiation.
